hook: Suh spent over 23 years at IBM, rising to head global strategic partnerships worth more than $10 billion before leading Watson AI product units in commerce, supply chain and collaboration; she then served as President of DocuSign and on its board through its 2018 IPO before becoming CEO of Niantic Spatial, a company building real-world foundation models for physical AI.
name: Inhi Cho Suh

quote.text: Inhi is bridging the gap between digital AI and physical AI for complex work in the real world.

reading.body:
Inhi Cho Suh's career traces a continuous line from enterprise data infrastructure to physical AI, making her one of the few executives whose operational record spans both the software foundations and the emerging frontier of real-world machine perception.

Her IBM years were not a single role but a sequence of distinct bets: database and data warehouse products, then big data portfolios including Hadoop and stream computing, then over $18 billion in analytics investments and acquisitions, then Watson applications for commerce and supply chain, and finally global partnerships exceeding $10 billion in revenue. Each move added a layer, from product management to P&L ownership to capital allocation to ecosystem scale. The DocuSign presidency, where she held Section 16 officer status overseeing product, engineering, design, and customer support, added a different kind of accountability, that of a public company operating unit rather than a division inside a larger conglomerate.

Niantic Spatial is the current destination, and the mission, building real-world foundation models for people, AI agents, and robots, represents the physical-AI thesis in its most direct form. Foundation models trained on physical-world data require sensors, compute, and infrastructure that differ meaningfully from cloud language models, though the data here does not specify what compute or power commitments Niantic Spatial has made. What the record does establish is that Suh has managed large-scale data systems, negotiated major technology partnerships, and led engineering organizations, a combination of skills that the physical-AI buildout, wherever it ultimately sits on the infrastructure stack, will require.
